posts.author: La Región en Línea
posts.snippet:
*El primer minuto es clave para frenar una extorsión telefónica*

• _Evita proporcionar información y verifica directamente con familiares para evitar realizar pagos a delincuentes_

*Morelia, Michoacán, 19 de agosto de 2026.-* La Secretaría de Seguridad Pública (SSP) recomienda mantener la calma durante el primer minuto de una llamada extorsiva para tomar el control de la situación, proteger tu información personal y colgar de inmediato ante cualquier amenaza o exigencia de dinero.

Los extorsionadores buscan generar miedo, presión y urgencia desde el inicio de la llamada para impedir que la víctima tenga tiempo de verificar la información. Entre las modalidades más frecuentes se encuentran amenazas contra familiares, supuestos secuestros o detenciones, así como exigencias de depósitos o transferencias a cambio de no causar algún daño.

La SSP recomienda en estos casos que no se no confirmen nombres, domicilios, lugares de trabajo, información bancaria o datos de familiares. La acción inmediata debe ser colgar y comunicarse directamente con la persona que supuestamente se encuentra en riesgo, utilizando más de una vía de contacto cuando sea necesario.

Como herramienta adicional de prevención, la aplicación 911 Michoacán cuenta con un identificador de llamadas enlazado con bases de datos de números relacionados con posibles actividades de extorsión, lo que permite generar alertas para advertir al usuario cuando recibe una comunicación sospechosa.

Además, desde la aplicación se puede solicitar apoyo ante una emergencia; al tocar el botón central con el logotipo del 911 se enlaza directamente la llamada con el servicio de emergencias. La plataforma también cuenta con apartados para reportar delitos, accidentes, incendios y situaciones de salud, además de permitir compartir la ubicación.

Ante una llamada sospechosa, la recomendación es clara: no deposites, no proporciones información, cuelga, verifica y marca 089 para realizar una denuncia anónima. Actuar desde el primer minuto puede evitar que una amenaza telefónica se convierta en una afectación económica.

posts.title: Na análise, identifico uma sopa de dados publicados de forma isolada, mas se eu analisá-los no conjunto concluo que teremos um efeito de saturação micro e macroeconômica.
posts.author: Vanderlei C.
posts.snippet:
Na análise, identifico uma sopa de dados publicados de forma isolada, mas se eu analisá-los no conjunto concluo que teremos um efeito de saturação micro e macroeconômica.
Vou postar nos comentários os conceitos:

A deflação que o mercado comemora não é sinal de saúde. É sinal de socorro.
O IGP-M registrou recuo de 0,36% na segunda prévia de agosto, desacelerando a deflação do mês anterior. Para a leitura apressada das manchetes, o dado sugere "acomodação" ou "estabilização". Na realidade operacional de quem produz e vende, o diagnóstico é outro: o paciente continua na UTI, e o respiro veio do aperto forçado de margem.

A margem do setor produtivo é espremida não por abundância de oferta, mas porque a economia real travou. Para conseguir girar estoque e honrar compromissos básicos, o empresário corta o próprio lucro na carne. É o "respiro" imediato de quem tenta sobreviver, mas que logo colide com uma conta impossível de pagar: a taxa de juros no topo do ciclo.
Se conectarmos os pontos da "sopa de dados" que o mercado insiste em analisar de forma fatiada, o indicador síntese é o de uma economia saturada e com elevado risco de colapso estrutural:

O Fechamento de Margens e o Aumento de Risco: A deflação no produtor e no consumidor é a prova da incapacidade de repassar custos. Quando o resultado operacional não cobre mais o custo do capital, o balanço corrói e o destino final vira o avanço alarmante das recuperações judiciais.

A "Gangorra" Incompatível: O governo mantém uma expansão fiscal para injetar liquidez artificial no consumo, enquanto o Banco Central é forçado a manter o aperto monetário rigoroso para combater essa mesma pressão. A mola estica, retrai e estrangula o setor privado no meio do caminho.

A Ilusão do Capital Especulativo: O juro alto atrai o carry trade — o capital de oportunidade que busca retorno financeiro rápido sem gerar um único emprego ou investimento em infraestrutura (CAPEX). Esse movimento mascara a verdadeira temperatura da economia.

A Fuga do Capital Produtivo (Precificação de Risco): Quem produz e detém visão de longo prazo já precificou o risco sistêmico. A fuga de divisas e a busca por estruturas offshores ou jurisdições defensivas refletem uma decisão simples: o investidor prefere garantir o patrimônio com retornos moderados lá fora a arriscar o principal em um ambiente de insolvência fiscal e incerteza institucional.

O Retardo da Economia Real: Os 11 pregões consecutivos de queda na bolsa e a revisão para baixo do dinamismo do PIB não são surpresas; são a confirmação tardia do arrocho monetário atuando sobre a capacidade produtiva.

Analisar um índice de preços isoladamente é como olhar a temperatura do paciente e ignorar que os órgãos estão parando. O Brasil vive a ausência de um planejamento macroeconômico de longo prazo, onde o socorro temporário da margem não será suficiente para sustentar o custo do dinheiro por muito tempo.

posts.title: ¿Quién acompaña a quienes tienen la responsabilidad de acompañar a otros?
posts.author: Adriana Silva Corres
posts.snippet:
¿Quién acompaña a quienes tienen la responsabilidad de acompañar a otros?
 
Hoy estaba leyendo la guía “Manager Development: What It Is, Why It Matters and How It Works”, de Gallup, encontré varias ideas que me hicieron mucho sentido por algunas situaciones que he estado viviendo esta semana…
 
A veces damos por hecho que, por ocupar una posición de liderazgo, una persona ya debería saber cómo desarrollar a su equipo, generar confianza, dar claridad, manejar conflictos, motivar, dar seguimiento…entre otras.
 
Pero liderar también se aprende y se sigue aprendiendo.
 
Cuando un líder necesita fortalecerse y no encuentra el apoyo para hacerlo, el impacto no se queda solo en él. Se empieza a notar en el equipo, en su dinámica, en la confianza y en la manera en que las personas viven su día a día.
 
Al mismo tiempo, se necesitan líderes con la apertura de reconocer que hay algo que necesitan trabajar, buscar apoyo y permitirse ser acompañados.
 
Gallup plantea que el desarrollo de los líderes necesita ser un proceso continuo, no algo que sucede una sola vez.
 
Y creo que ahí hay algo importante: necesitamos líderes dispuestos a seguir desarrollándose, pero también organizaciones dispuestas a acompañarlos en ese proceso.
 
Porque cuando un líder crece, el impacto difícilmente termina en él, también llega a su equipo.

posts.author: Jim Mueller

Q: What’s the scariest AI security risk most companies are ignoring right now?

A: Unmanaged AI use : employees feeding sensitive company data into tools your security team cannot see, control, or audit.

This is shadow AI. It can expose customer records, intellectual property, financial information, credentials, and confidential strategy in seconds.

The danger isn’t limited to a breach. Once sensitive data enters the wrong AI environment, you may lose control over where it is stored, how it is processed, and whether it is used to improve a model.

The fix is not banning AI. That rarely works.

The fix: establish approved tools, enforce data-handling rules, control access, monitor usage, and train employees on what must never be entered into an AI system.

AI adoption is accelerating. Security cannot remain an afterthought.

posts.title: Got an AI Trust Issue
posts.author: Richard Stoner
posts.snippet:
Got an AI Trust Issue
Gem advice:
Your skepticism isn't just reasonable—it is the healthiest posture to have right now. The AI market is currently flooded with hundreds of venture-backed clones and "wrapper" apps that take a base model, slap a slick interface on it, and aggressively market it as the next breakthrough.
When you are deciding whether to type even a single prompt into a new platform, the risks break down into three distinct areas:
1. The Middleman Problem (Data Privacy)
 * Major Platforms (OpenAI, Google): While not immune to criticism, established tech companies have public-facing compliance frameworks (SOC 2, ISO certifications, GDPR/CCPA alignment) and clear toggles to opt out of training on your data.
 * New / Unknown Apps: Smaller startups and browser extensions frequently act as middlemen. When you ask them a question, your query may be logged in an unencrypted database, routed through multiple third-party servers, or harvested to build user behavioral profiles before it ever reaches an actual AI model.
2. The Wrapper Reality
Most new AI apps on app stores aren't running novel intelligence—they are literally renting access to OpenAI, Anthropic, or open-source models via API. You aren't getting new technology; you are simply giving a third party an extra layer of visibility into your queries and paying a markup for it.
3. The "Zero-Trust" Prompting Rule
You do not need to blindly trust any platform if you adopt a simple operational rule for what you feed them:
 * Safe for any vetted tool: General concepts, coding logic, grammar restructuring, public research, creative brainstorming, and hypothetical scenarios.
 * Never feed into any tool (major or minor): Personal identifiable information (passwords, SSNs, phone numbers), proprietary corporate data, unreleased intellectual property, or confidential client records.
How to Handle the Noise
Stick to your core tools. You don't owe any new app your attention, your download, or your data just because it launched with flashy marketing. If a tool doesn't offer a transparent privacy policy, clear enterprise data handling, and an obvious value you can't already get from your primary assistants, ignoring it completely is the right move.

posts.title: What if the most honest signal in crypto isn't price, volume, or fees — but how much supply holders have voluntarily locked up?
posts.author: Moazzam Khoja, Ph.D., CFA
posts.snippet:
What if the most honest signal in crypto isn't price, volume, or fees — but how much supply holders have voluntarily locked up?

We call it the conviction ratio (λ): the share of a crypto asset's supply that holders have staked or locked. It's observable on-chain, in real time, for free. We tested whether it prices the cross-section of crypto returns across 24 proof-of-stake coins and 101 DeFi tokens, 2015–2026.

Three findings for practitioners:
1️⃣ For coins (L1s like ETH, SOL, ADA): conviction alone tells you nothing. Conviction conditional on valuation tells you a lot. High staking in a cheap coin (by growth-adjusted NVT) predicts outperformance. High staking in an expensive coin is the worst bucket — that's a staking-yield trap, and the effect is strong (t ≈ 3.5, surviving a 12-signal horse race).
2️⃣ For tokens (DeFi/governance): conviction works standalone, but only at the extremes. A top-vs-bottom quintile portfolio earned ~1.7%/month factor-adjusted alpha that no competing signal spans. And the long side isn't where the action is: the practical use is an exclusion screen — the low-conviction quintile reliably underperforms.
3️⃣ It survived everything we threw at it: NVT, Metcalfe, stock-to-flow scarcity, price-to-fees, momentum, reversal, volatility, technicals. We also report what failed — the coin-level signal alone, and our quadrant strategy — because nulls are information too.

How this paper was made: it was submitted to the American Finance Association's 2027 special session on research written with generative AI. Claude (Anthropic) did ~95% of the work — literature review, theory drafting, all data engineering and estimation, writing. I made the calls: which hypotheses, which measures, what to keep, what to kill. Every AI conversation — 1,500+ pages, from the initial prompt to submission — is published as an appendix, with all code and data on GitHub. My takeaway: AI multiplies a researcher; it doesn't replace one. The judgment layer is still the scarce input.

DIGITAL FINANCIAL INFRASTRUCTURE — DAY 07

I continued reading EY’s “Token Due Diligence: A Structured Approach to Evaluate Digital Asset Risk”

Yesterday, I was trying to understand the paper from the perspective of tokenomics, governance, value capture, and how different types of tokens can create different economic rights. Today, I finished the paper, and the bigger picture became much clearer.

What I found most interesting is that the paper is not really trying to answer “Is this token a good investment?”

It is asking a much more useful question:
How do you systematically understand the risks behind a digital asset?
A blockchain ecosystem can combine technology, token economics, governance, users, developers, liquidity, regulation and cybersecurity in ways that create very different risk profiles.

The framework breaks this down across areas such as strategic and reputational risk, technical risk, financial risk, legal and compliance risk, cybersecurity, and auditability.

The part I keep coming back to is the relationship between these layers.
For example, a token may have strong utility, but how is that utility actually connected to economic value? Who captures the revenue? How does the token supply change over time? Who controls governance? How decentralized is the underlying protocol? And can the activity actually be verified through on chain data?

Those questions make me realize that understanding digital assets requires more than understanding crypto markets.
It requires thinking across finance + technology + risk + data.

That is exactly the direction I am trying to explore through my Digital Financial Infrastructure journey.
Finance → markets, lending, collateral, liquidity and risk
Technology → blockchain, smart contracts, tokenization and DeFi
Analytics → on chain data, financial analysis, BI and eventually AI

I also liked the paper's conclusion that the framework isn't designed to predict which token will succeed. Its purpose is to help identify risks and ask better questions before making decisions. Credits to the co-author of the paper Mark Vangeloff, CISA

That is probably the biggest takeaway for me so far.
I'm still very early in this journey, but I'm starting to see how the pieces connect.

Next, I want to move from understanding the framework → applying it to actual protocols and tokens → analyzing the underlying data.
One financial mechanism at a time.

Commercial real estate is one of the largest asset classes on earth. Most people will never own a square foot of it because the wrapper doesn't exist. Minimum tickets is in the hundreds of thousands and the hold periods measured in years. The closing process also runs on couriers and filing cabinets.

Blockstar Corporation is building for that gap. The model is commercial properties held inside legal structures, trusts and SPVs, with tokens representing fractional interests in those entities. Ownership rights and obligations are tracked as separate, timestamped records rather than bundled into contracts that need re-negotiating every time a lease changes. Compliance and KYC is enforced at the protocol layer instead of bolted on afterward.

What I find interesting is where the idea came from. Blockstar's founder John Everest Thomas spent 25 years in traditional real estate before this, then 18 months on the road across 16 countries executing property transactions structured around crypto. This is not a crypto team discovering real estate but a real estate operator who got tired of watching good assets sit illiquid, and went looking for a better wrapper.

That ordering matters in RWA. The projects that struggle are usually the ones that understand the token and not the building. posts.title: Two tokens can have the same name and nothing else in common.
posts.author: CT Academy
posts.snippet:
Two tokens can have the same name and nothing else in common.

Anyone can create a token and call it whatever they like. There is no register, no uniqueness rule and no approval step. So on a wallet with any history you will find entries that read identically and are entirely different assets.

That matters the moment you make a manual adjustment. If you search by name and pick from a dropdown, you may be correcting the balance on a token the client never touched, while the one you meant to fix stays wrong. Nothing errors. The file just quietly says something untrue.

The identity that counts is the contract address. It is unique, it is on the blockchain, and it is what the software is actually tracking underneath the label it shows you.

So before any manual entry on a token: find it on a blockchain explorer, confirm the contract address matches the transaction you are correcting, and work from that rather than the name.

It adds a minute. It removes a category of error that is very hard to find afterwards, because nothing about the file looks wrong.

SEC unveils new crypto rules hailed as a win for the digital asset industry

The US Securities and Exchange Commission has proposed a sweeping new framework for crypto assets, offering firms two clear paths to raise money without full securities registration. Industry groups have broadly welcomed the plan, calling its terms considerably more generous than anticipated.

The SEC announced on Tuesday that it had filed a proposal titled "Regulation Crypto Assets", giving crypto entrepreneurs a clearer, considerably lighter route to raising capital under federal securities law, according to the press release published by the regulator.

It is the agency's first formal rulemaking dedicated to crypto asset offerings, building on broader interpretive guidance the SEC issued in March, and would spare qualifying issuers the costly registration process required of most public offerings.

At the centre of the proposal sit two new exemptions.

The "startup exemption" would let an issuer raise up to $5 million (€4.3mn) over a four year period without registering the offering.

A second, the "fundraising exemption", would permit raises of up to $75 million (€64.7mn) within any 12 month stretch, though issuers relying on it would still need to publish financial statements and meet ongoing reporting duties.

"We're a small startup, DPDP doesn't apply to us."

This is the #1 myth we hear — and it's wrong.

So you're probably thinking — okay, what even is DPDP? Let's break it down in simple terms.

The DPDP Act, 2023 is the Indian government's big step toward protecting your digital data privacy.

Your name. Your number. Your browsing behavior. Your habits, tracked silently by websites you've probably never even heard of.

For years, that data was collected first, questions asked never.

DPDP changes the rule of the game: your data, your choice.

And there's no size exemption. If your website collects even a name, email, phone number, or tracking cookie from Indian users — this law applies to you. Startup, solo founder, enterprise — doesn't matter.

What that actually means for your business:

posts.title: 🚨 The SEC just proposed a new federal framework for crypto-asset capital formation.
posts.author: Allen Branch
posts.snippet:
🚨 The SEC just proposed a new federal framework for crypto-asset capital formation.

If adopted, Regulation Crypto Assets could mark one of the clearest moves yet away from regulation-by-enforcement—and toward a structured path for builders to raise capital in the U.S. 🇺🇸⚖️

Here is the breakdown:

🏗️ Rule 200: Startup runway
Projects could raise up to $5M over four years without registering a traditional securities offering—using streamlined EDGAR filings at the start and finish.

💰 Rules 300–307: Scaled fundraising
A Regulation A-style capital ladder:
• Tier 1: Up to 20M∗∗in12months•∗∗Tier2:∗∗Upto∗∗
20M∗∗in12months•∗∗Tier2:∗∗Upto∗∗75M, with audited financials and continuing SEC reporting

📋 Rule 103: Say what you are building
Plain-English disclosure on the network, product, roadmap, governance, insiders, risks, and use of proceeds. Less mythology. More accountability. 🧾

🚫 Rule 104: Bad actors stay out
Fraud convictions, SEC bars, and similar disqualifying events would block access to these exemptions. Investor protection remains central. 🛡️

🔓 Rule 400: The potential game changer
A proposed pathway for an issuer to certify that it has completed—or permanently ceased—the essential managerial work promised to investors.
Translation: a clearer framework for when the investment contract may end, rather than leaving the industry to guess indefinitely. 🚦

🏛️ Rule 500: One federal framework
For qualifying offerings and secondary trades, federal rules would preempt state registration and qualification requirements while filings remain current.
That could reduce the 50-state compliance maze that has slowed legitimate U.S. innovation for years. 🗺️➡️🛣️
⚠️ Importantly, anti-fraud and anti-manipulation protections would remain fully in force. Innovation does not mean a free pass.

The real takeaway:
Crypto entrepreneurs may finally get a more visible capital-formation ladder—from early-stage token launches to regulated, scaled offerings—without having to choose between moving offshore and operating in ambiguity.

This is only a proposal, and comments will be due 60 days after Federal Register publication. But strategically, it signals a meaningful shift:
The U.S. may be moving from asking, “Is this a security?” to also providing a process for how compliant crypto markets can be built.

For tokenized assets, stablecoins, DeFi infrastructure, and onchain AI, the regulatory geography is changing fast. 🌐📈

What matters most now: whether the final rules preserve a workable path for real builders—not just the biggest incumbents.

posts.title: The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) of the United Kingdom has announced the closing of a multi-year chapter of uncertainty concerning the UK cryptocurrency policy by outlining fi
posts.author: Prifinance International
posts.snippet:
The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) of the United Kingdom has announced the closing of a multi-year chapter of uncertainty concerning the UK cryptocurrency policy by outlining five policy statements (PS26/9, PS26/10, PS26/11, PS26/12, and PS26/13) together with finalized guidance outlining the first complete regulation concerning cryptocurrencies in the country.

The scope of the regulation is large as it is intended to include as many aspects relating to cryptocurrencies as possible. The regulation targets trading platforms, custody (this is provided through CASS 17 — a new chapter created specifically for client crypto assets), stablecoins, staking, lending, and dealing and arranging transactions. This becomes possible thanks to the consultations that took place in 2025 (CP25/14, CP25/15, CP25/25, and etc.) that resulted in the final rules instead of proposals.

There are two design decisions worth mentioning for people working in this field. The FCA has managed to take a rather lenient approach to the settlement float allowing 2% of the company’s own funds available for the operational liquidity management. Second, the custody laws are technology-agnostic as it concerns the private key management.

Although the effective date is October 25, 2027, which might create an impression of the remaining time, the companies should realize they won’t be able to build custody infrastructure meeting CASS 17 requirements, carry out adequate prudential capital planning, and make changes in the Senior Manager and Certification Regime mapping.

The first thing that needs to be done by the companies operating in the UK is the gap analysis: what requirements of the final custody regulation differ from the present situation and what changes are required for the prudential capital planning.

We are ready to offer consultancy services in terms of the FCA cryptoasset authorisation and CASS 17 readiness.

posts.title: Everyone's calling their Web3 project "the future of the internet."
posts.author: BAMISE FRANCIE
posts.snippet:
Everyone's calling their Web3 project "the future of the internet."

Almost none of them are.

I've watched dozens die. Some deserved it. A few didn't. And the difference was never the whitepaper, the hype, or the funding.

It was the work.

So here's how I spot a project that's actually building before the hype dies and the price dumps.

1. The code is public, and it's alive.

Commits this week, not six months ago. Real devs, real pull requests. I've seen teams with millions in funding and a codebase untouched since launch. That's a statue, not a project.

2. They talk about what they shipped, not what's "coming soon."

The graveyard of Web3 is full of "Q3 we'll launch." Real teams say "this broke, here's how we fixed it."


3. They take hard questions without getting mad.

Do they block you? Call you a "FUDster"? Or say "fair point, here's what we're doing"? Teams that hide flaws will hide worse.

4. There's a real product you can use.

Not a testnet with three buttons. Something that solves a problem you can actually feel.

5. They're boring in the best way.

The loudest projects are usually the emptiest. Real builders are deep in the work, not deep in your mentions.

My honest take? I've been burned by this space. I've believed in things that died. I still believe in what Web3 can be  I just stopped believing in what projects *say* they are.

Look at the work. Trust the receipts. Ignore the noise.

In February 2025, Italy's competition authority fined GLS Group - a logistics company - €8 million.
 
Not for emissions. For a "Climate Protect" sustainability program that was promoted without the transparency and diligence regulators expected from a high-emissions sector.
 
That case is not isolated, and it is not just Italy. Giorgio Armani was fined €3.5 million the same year after its ethical and social responsibility claims were contradicted by actual working conditions found at its suppliers. Shein was fined €1 million over recyclability claims. In Germany, a court banned Apple from advertising the Apple Watch as "CO2-neutral" because the offset scheme behind the claim did not hold up. In the Netherlands, a court ruled KLM's sustainable aviation fuel claims misleading.
 
This is the trend worth watching: ESG claims are no longer a reputational risk. They are a legal one, and the exposure now runs through your supply chain, not just your marketing department.
 
The UK's Competition and Markets Authority made this explicit in guidance published this January: companies are legally responsible for misleading environmental claims made anywhere in their supply chain - including claims that originate from suppliers, not just the ones a company makes directly. In the EU, the Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive starts applying in September 2026, banning vague claims like "eco-friendly" or "climate-friendly" unless backed by verifiable evidence, and it applies to brand names, packaging imagery, and offsetting claims, not just headline slogans.
 
The business impact is direct: fines up to 10% of global turnover under the UK's new consumer law powers, court orders to pull campaigns, and now, liability for claims your suppliers make that you never personally wrote.
 
The risk of not acting is not hypothetical anymore - it is a growing list of real companies, across fashion, aviation, tech, and logistics, that already paid for it.
 
What this means for Supply Chain leaders specifically: every sustainability claim your company makes now needs a data trail back to your actual operations and suppliers - not a script written by the marketing team. If a claim cannot survive an audit, it should not survive the ad campaign.
 
Is your company able to trace every ESG claim it makes back to verifiable supply chain data - or is that gap still open?

I was 20 minutes into a flight home from a conference. The app the conference used was not optimized for mobile; a poor decision for an event where you're constantly on the move! I connected to airplane WiFi, opened up Chrome DevTools out of curiosity and started poking around to see what it would take to make it mobile friendly.

Five minutes later, I had the name and email address of every single attendee. Ten minutes later, I could see what people had purchased, which panels they had attended, and even their home city/state. Things that I have to assume they thought were private. I certainly did!

I didn't "hack" anything. I didn't phish, I didn't sneak onto a server, I didn't rappel from the roof of a high rise into a secure room and stick a USB into a mainframe. It wasn't even a clever trick. The app's own network requests were just handing out this data like candy. Anyone with a web browser could've done what I did with zero technical background beyond "right-click, inspect."

I reported it. They patched it. As far as I can tell, no harm done.

But here's the part that sticks with me even today: this wasn't a scrappy weekend project. This was a vendor running ticketing and payments for an event doing over $2M in sales on a single event across ticketing and merch. That's real money using real people's data and real trust. And the leak was something any competent engineer could've taken an afternoon to catch. This could've cost them their biggest customer and possibly even gotten them into a lawsuit. Between GDPR and CCPA and myriad privacy laws, this could've been a company-ending fiasco.

I keep seeing this story play out in AI-built products. Teams ship features faster than ever, which is genuinely great. Armed with agentic coding tools, I ship code faster than I've ever shipped before -- and many former colleagues will tell you I'm a very fast programmer! 

But "the AI wrote it and it works" and "the AI wrote it and it's safe" are two totally, completely different claims. And I've watched people conflate them right up until it costs them their biggest customer, a headline in the news, or worse.

Look, being fast isn't the same as being competent. And crucially, shipping fast and shipping safely are not mutually exclusive. It just requires someone in the room who knows what to check.

One of the most important jobs of tech leaders isn't to slow things down or to create bureaucracy for the sake of it. It's to make sure "fast" and "safe" are the same word.

If you're shipping fast and want someone to sanity-check it before it becomes a headline, that's the kind of thing I do. Always happy to talk.

Blockchain rails do not replace banks; they give them a faster, cheaper settlement layer to compete instead of losing volume. If any bank wants to explore what that looks like, Beenco Labs is glad to help; no pitch attached.

Utility companies are another clear case, one of the most inefficiency-plagued sectors in the country, where smart contracts remove the discretion inefficiency has hidden behind. Corporate balance sheets carry value sitting static at historic cost, and tokenization gives that value an actual market. 

This is credible today because the legal groundwork exists. The Virtual Assets Act of 2026 gave Pakistan real legal architecture; PVARA now licenses providers, and the State Bank, SECP, and FBR are actively involved. Binance and HTX hold NOCs, Bitget is following, and Binance has signed an agreement to explore tokenizing up to $2B in sovereign bonds.

posts.title: "Fixing Prediction Markets: Unlocking Collective Intelligence Without the Sports Betting and Market Integrity Concerns"
posts.author: Colin Goldman
posts.snippet:
"Fixing Prediction Markets: Unlocking Collective Intelligence Without the Sports Betting and Market Integrity Concerns"

Our opinion piece today on PolyPunter lays out a succinct plan for reforming prediction markets and mitigating legal, political, and public backlash in a practical landscape where those factors matter. The promise of any new innovation always faces public scrutiny, whether legal or reputational. See AI data center controversies at the moment. We are a nation that leans toward free markets, but is undoubtedly bound by regulation and political majorities

There are five areas prediction markets could practically reform and enhance:

1. Deal with the "sports betting" legal and public perception hurdles by, first, extensively limiting federally regulated sports event contracts to a narrower game outcome and season-long futures window, excluding all props and ancillary or whimsical event contracts. Additionally, restrict marketing and design to avoid clearly mimicking sportsbooks' activity. (The alternative is to spin-out the sports and entertainment events markets to a separate prediction platform entity that negotiates separate deals with each state gaming authority).

2. Move liquidity from high-volume recreational events markets to subsidize fluidity in markets with greater social utility. Make the mission to enable the underlying promise of prediction markets for accurate pricing signals in key derivatives markets used for hedging risk, business forecasting, scientific advancement, and public policy guidance. 

3. Internally self-ban all morally hazardous markets such as criminal events, world leader assassinations, and military-related casualties. 

4. Dramatically ramp up market integrity and enforcement actions to mitigate insider trading, market manipulation, market resolution rules conflicts, and transparency in trading and accounts. This becomes a challenge on crypto-native platforms but is doable and should be the standard for any U.S.-registered exchange. 

5. Dramatically ramp up educational and informational content and standards for retail traders, including sharing user-segment data on expected returns/losses. This also includes far more promotion of responsible trading and addiction-related tools and services.

Much of this is being done already, at least in some measure, sometimes token measures, by either the platforms themselves or as a result of CFTC certification and regulatory standards. But more emphasis is needed, and certainly a solution, ideally a proactive solution ahead of Congress and the courts, for solving the "sports betting" cloud which hangs over all else (while notably also providing the bulk of trading volume in the present day, so not so simple).

posts.title: A lot is moving in this space, and it is not always converging. What I keep noticing is that the permissive outcomes are landing on the training act, not on acquisition. How you go
posts.author: Mircea Farcau
posts.snippet:
A lot is moving in this space, and it is not always converging. What I keep noticing is that the permissive outcomes are landing on the training act, not on acquisition. How you got the data can decide the economics even where the use itself is defensible, and that holds whichever way the exceptions and the case law resolve.

Also, the chart doesn't tell the whole story. The data most likely to make a model right and trustworthy (especially in science, law, and finance) never left the "institution" that produced it, and privity is probably the biggest reason. In a chain of good old bilateral licenses, each promise runs only between its own two parties. The party a rights holder most needs to constrain is the end user (AI developer, in most cases), two or more links away, and that is exactly the party it has no relationship with. Getting to a remedy means working through every agreement in between, each with its own caps, carve-outs, forum, and balance sheet/insolvency risks. Faced with that, licensing nothing could be a defensible decision. Price matters, obviously, everyone wants to get paid, but no number truly compensates for a promise you cannot enforce.

I believe the fix is not a new exception or legislative measure. Third-party enforcement rights already exist in most developed systems, and flow-down terms have been routine in software sublicensing for decades. What almost nobody has done is build them systematically, across many holders and many recipients, in a form that holds up in whatever jurisdiction they sit in. 

That is the data layer we are building at Redpine. More on this to come.

System-generated errors may lead to penalty waivers, subject to the law, and affected taxpayers have been advised to retain evidence such as screenshots and support tickets.

LOGBOOK | 04 of 10

How are leading organizations managing risk today?

Not by looking at risks in isolation.

The more I deepen my work in risk analysis, the clearer one principle becomes: risk management only creates real value when it is connected to organizational objectives.

A risk does not exist in isolation.

Its relevance depends on what the organization is trying to achieve, the environment in which it operates, and how internal and external conditions may affect those objectives.

This is where a holistic approach becomes essential.

Rather than focusing exclusively on individual operational risks, mature organizations continuously scan their environment, connect emerging threats and opportunities, and assess how changes may influence their overall risk profile.

Economic shifts.
Regulatory changes.
Technology.
Operational pressures.
People.
Culture.
Environmental and geopolitical factors.

Individually, they may appear manageable.

Together, they can significantly change the conditions under which an organization operates.

This is why environmental scanning should not be treated as a one-time exercise.

Periodic reviews often every six to twelve months, or whenever significant changes occur allow organizations to reassess assumptions, priorities and exposures against their strategic objectives.

Because ultimately, the question is not simply:

“What risks do we have?”

It is:

“What could affect our ability to achieve our objectives?”

That shift in perspective is where Risk Management moves beyond control and becomes part of strategy, governance and organizational resilience.

Marina Bay Sands was fined S$243,096 for a data breach in 2025. Singapore's PDPA now treats AI data governance as a board-level liability — and for large organisations, penalties can reach 10% of annual Singapore turnover. If your firm uses personal data in AI training, this is not a question of best practice. It is a compliance obligation.

The Far East's AI regulatory landscape is moving fast, and the implications for international professional services businesses are significant.

Singapore's IMDA has published its Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (updated May 2026), addressing autonomous AI systems that don't just advise — they act. The PDPC's final Advisory Guidelines on Generative AI (July 2026) extend PDPA obligations to organisations collecting and curating training datasets. AI systems must have accountable owners, training data must be documented, and incident response plans must be in place.

Elsewhere in the region, Japan's dedicated AI Act came into full effect in September 2025, with APPI amendments on the horizon that will reshape how personal data can be used in AI development. South Korea's AI Basic Act entered into force in January 2026, introducing mandatory impact assessments and user notification requirements for high-impact AI systems.

The clear takeaway for global enterprises: regional AI compliance is no longer a secondary consideration. Firms operating across Singapore, Japan, and South Korea must audit their AI governance frameworks now — covering training data, vendor contracts, agentic systems, and cross-border data flows — before enforcement catches up with them.

Ops Intel helps professional services businesses navigate exactly this complexity.

#AICompliance #AIRegulation #BusinessCompliance #DataProtection #ResponsibleAI

posts.title: In a bold political statement, Ukraine’s former Defence Mykhailo Fedorov - whose recent dismissal sparked protests across the country - announced the need of wartime elections.
posts.author: Dr Jaroslava Barbieri
posts.snippet:
In a bold political statement, Ukraine’s former Defence Mykhailo Fedorov - whose recent dismissal sparked protests across the country - announced the need of wartime elections.

His statement centres around three key concepts: responsibility, justice, and hope. 

▪️Responsibility is the political equivalent of his signature data-driven approach to war. Leaders must deliver tangible, measurable results. Without elections, a culture of impunity consolidates. Officials stop fearing accountability when they cannot be voted out.

▪️Justice amplifies the mounting sense of injustice in Ukrainian society. On one side are soldiers who cannot return home, alongside civilians suffering and dying daily; on the other are officials accused of corruption for whom a prolonged war provides further opportunities for self-enrichment that directly undermine the war effort.

▪️Hope reflects the belief that Ukraine can win and thrive as a nation if accountable leaders produce results and report directly to society. While Fedorov’s focus on tech-driven, asymmetric warfare initially gave people hope that Ukraine could turn the tide and bring the war toward an end, that optimism has faded. As Ukrsine faces severe air defence shortages, Russia’s heavy reliance on ballistic missile strikes has left many feeling that there’s no end in sight.

This is an exceptionally risky move on Fedorov’s part. Recent data from the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) shows that a clear majority of Ukrainians (57%) still do not believe elections should take place right now. Most citizens continue to insist that elections should be postponed until after the war ends.

The primary reasons why wartime elections remain nearly impossible to execute:

▫️Ukrainian law explicitly bans elections under martial law to ensure stability during wartime.
▫️Martial law restrictions make equal access to information nearly impossible. Opposition parties and new political movements lack equal platform visibility, balanced media access, and the financial resources required to mount a fair campaign.
▫️Opening the political arena during a period of extreme social vulnerability risks fueling populist polarization, which Russia would actively weaponize to fracture national unity and destabilize society from within.
▫️Conducting safe voting processes while under constant bombardment poses extreme risks to civilian lives.
▫️Millions of active-duty soldiers on the front lines would be unable to fairly run as candidates or safely cast their ballots.
▫️Millions of Ukrainians remain internally displaced or refugees abroad, while large swathes of territory remain under Russian occupation, crippling electoral integrity.

If you’ve missed it, watch the recording of our recent discussion Chatham House Russia and Eurasia Programme on these key challenges for Ukraine’s democracy in wartime 👇

posts.title: * The "Experience Paradox": Why Politicians Age In, but Tech Experts Age Out*
posts.author: Dr. Krishna Murari
posts.snippet:
* The "Experience Paradox": Why Politicians Age In, but Tech Experts Age Out*

Why can a politician lead a nation at 75+, while a brilliant aerospace designer is forced to retire at 60? It is a fascinating systemic contradiction that highlights how different industries define and value human capability.
The Political Longevity Formula
In politics, advanced age is often treated as an asset. Backed by world-class healthcare and dedicated support staffs, senior leaders are insulated from physical burnout. Their daily work focuses entirely on human psychology, negotiation, and strategic influence—skills that do not become obsolete with technology. Because democratic constitutions prioritize voter choice over rigid corporate rules, there are no retirement caps or degree requirements. The system is designed to let voters judge a leader's mental fitness at the ballot box.
The Corporate and PSU Stagnation Bottleneck
In government organizations and PSUs, the rules are drastically different. Enforced retirement ages (typically 58 to 60) exist to keep the system healthy. Without predictable exits, younger professionals face career bottlenecks, and organizations cannot inject fresh talent into the workforce. Furthermore, standard labor laws require uniform rules to avoid legal chaos, making individual fitness evaluations impractical on a mass scale.
The Aerospace Exception and the Private Pivot
While rapid software shifts can favor younger minds, sectors like aerospace and defence rely on institutional physics, structural intuition, and legacy safety data. You cannot code away the laws of metallurgy or fluid dynamics; that requires decades of design experience.
Because strict DoPT guidelines cap public consultancies at age 63 to 65 to prevent stagnation, a massive structural shift has occurred. Private defence giants and aerospace consortia are actively headhunting these retired master designers. Free from government age caps, these 70+ year-old veterans now serve as Chief Technical Advisors in the private sector. They guide our national defense projects under corporate banners, proving that true expertise never actually retires.
The Solution: A Case for Fitness-Based Extensions
To prevent this critical brain drain from our important organisations of the country like ISRO, DRDO, HAL, BEL, ADA, NAL etc., it is time to rethink rigid retirement caps. For specialized, deep-tech roles, we should introduce a system of merit-based extensions supported by mandatory, rigorous physical and cognitive medical examinations. This balanced approach would allow healthy, sharp master designers to continue serving the nation directly within government frameworks, ensuring that invaluable institutional wisdom is not prematurely pushed out the door.

posts.title: How do we regulate AI when we haven’t yet worked out how to regulate the corporations building it? Consider how quickly a handful of technology companies have accumulated extraordi
posts.author: Juncture: Dialogues on Inclusive Capitalism
posts.snippet:
How do we regulate AI when we haven’t yet worked out how to regulate the corporations building it? Consider how quickly a handful of technology companies have accumulated extraordinary amounts of capital, data, infrastructure, talent and political influence. 

How have these Big Tech platforms become so powerful and so quickly? How can they be regulated?

These questions were considered at a recent event at the University of Auckland Business School organised by Aotearoa Centre for Leadership and Governance with Professor Susan Watson, Matt Bartlett, Dr. Jonathan Hardman and Dr. Lynn Buckley.

According to Susan Watson, part of the answer may lie in something we rarely talk about: corporations can own other forms of capital — including other corporations.

Call it "recursive capital": capital owning capital, which can then own more capital. This creates a powerful compounding mechanism. 

A corporation can grow horizontally and vertically, acquire competitors, build subsidiaries, control infrastructure and accumulate assets in ways that other forms of companies cannot.

Corporations can also make claims on future capital, like data before we fully understood its economic value. 

The companies developing AI aren't simply selling another product. They are competing to build a technology that could shape labour, education, healthcare, media, defence, infrastructure and much of the economy.

If we look at the corporate structures driving AI development, and dive into history, we can find some uncomfortable parallels.

The East India Company accumulated commercial, military and political power on a staggering scale.

The Gilded Age produced corporations whose control over oil, steel, railroads and other infrastructure became so concentrated that governments eventually developed new forms of antitrust regulation to constrain them.

We have seen before what happens when corporate structures are allowed to compound capital, control and political influence faster than governing institutions can respond.

So we really need to ask: “What should the law allow the corporations developing AI to own, control, acquire and extract?”

The state created the legal architecture that gives corporations many of the powers they possess in the first place and it can also reshape and reform these powers.

Corporate personhood, limited liability, ownership rights, mergers, subsidiaries, intellectual property and many of the other mechanisms that enable corporate accumulation are ultimately products of law.

We shouldn't treat the current distribution of corporate power as inevitable. It was designed, and what law has helped create, law can change.

The challenge is to do that before AI companies become too deeply embedded in our economy and institutions.

#FutureOfCapitalism #Juncture #InclusiveCapitalism #CorporateGovernance #BigTech

comments.text: The regulatory gap is even sharper once you add sector rules like the AI Act's risk tiers on top of general corporate law — a high-risk AI system can sit inside a corporate structure that antitrust and company law were never designed to see, let alone the compounding ownership problem you describe.

If recursive capital is the mechanism, does regulation need to intervene at the level of corporate structure itself, rather than at the level of the specific product or model, the way antitrust eventually did with the Gilded Age conglomerates?

Working with deep tech and defence founders, we see early on how quickly a cap table and a set of subsidiary structures can start doing exactly what you describe — accumulating optionality and control well before any AI-specific regulation would even apply.

posts.title: Until recently, it seemed that AI had given everyone the ability to become a makeshift "Stephen King", "Ernest Hemingway", or "J.K. Rowling". It appears that era is quietly drawing
posts.author: Serhiy Dzis
posts.snippet:
Until recently, it seemed that AI had given everyone the ability to become a makeshift "Stephen King", "Ernest Hemingway", or "J.K. Rowling". It appears that era is quietly drawing to a close.

I have recently observed an intriguing shift: ChatGPT is increasingly refusing prompts to generate text in the exact style of prominent authors. Instead of direct imitation, it now offers to craft something with a similar atmosphere or mood, but in its own distinct voice. The driving force behind this restriction is copyright law, which is finally formulating a practical response to the challenges posed by generative AI.

OpenAI is currently defending itself against a wave of litigation initiated by writers and rightsholders. A core argument from the plaintiffs is that the AI is capable of reproducing texts that are uncomfortably close to original, copyrighted works. While traditional IP law does not protect "style" per se, the boundary between stylistic imitation and the actual reproduction of creative expression is becoming remarkably thin.

These legal disputes are doing something unprecedented: they are influencing not only corporate legal strategies but the underlying architecture of the technologies themselves. Lawsuits are no longer merely shaping case law - they are actively altering algorithmic behaviour.

This is exactly why I disagree with the prevailing narrative that copyright will become obsolete in the age of AI. On the contrary, a well-structured legal defence strategy is proving powerful enough to dictate terms to the world's largest tech platforms.

The key metric to monitor over the next few years will be exactly where courts draw the line between inspiration, imitation, and direct copyright infringement.
posts.reason: Copyright and generative AI legal disputes directly engage with tech law and regulatory change, speaking to founders and deep tech companies navigating IP questions.

comments.text: Worth noting that this litigation pressure is doing something copyright doctrine alone rarely does — style is not protected, but the moment output reproduces protectable expression the line moves from an abstract fair-use debate to a concrete product design constraint, which is exactly why OpenAI is engineering around it rather than waiting for a ruling.

Do you think courts will end up drawing the inspiration/infringement line based on output similarity case by case, or will legislatures eventually codify a stylistic-imitation threshold the way some jurisdictions did with database rights?

We see the same dynamic in white paper and marketing material review for tech clients — once litigation risk becomes real, the safest technical architecture is usually built well before any court actually rules, exactly as you describe with ChatGPT's behaviour shift.
